Learning Objectives
Describe the initial assessment of the limb at risk of amputation.
Explain common misconceptions about deciding whether to perform limb salvage or
amputation after trauma.
Identify appropriate preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative plans to optimize
recovery after amputation.
Discuss common complications after amputation because of trauma.

The postoperative course after trauma-related amputation must be optimized, with
amputation being considered a reconstruction procedure rather than an ablative
procedure. As many as 30% of patients who undergo trauma-related amputation are re-
hospitalized, with 15% requiring revision of the residual limb.1 Of patients who
experience a major upper extremity amputation, 31% will require at least one revision
surgery.2
Epidemiology
Traumatic lower limb amputations account for approximately 16% of overall amputations per
year.3,4
Approximately 20,000 new lower limb amputations occur each year because of trauma.3,4
The prevalence of major upper extremity amputations performed for trauma is approximately
one-third that of the lower extremity.3
Traumatic amputations of the hand and fingers affect approximately 25,000 individuals per
year, a figure that has remained constant over the past 20 years.

Epidemiology
Approximately 1.6 million people are living in the United States with limb loss, and
although only 16% of annual amputations are the result of trauma, more than 45% of
those living with an amputation have it because of trauma.3 This is because the
population that sustains amputations from trauma typically is young.
Only 8% of individuals living with an amputation have a major upper extremity
amputation (excluding the fingers). The most common level is through the humerus
(35%), followed by the forearm (30%) and the hand (14%).2 Finger amputations occur in a
bimodal distribution (children younger than 5 years and elderly older than 65 years). An
estimated 45,000 digital amputations occur in the United States each year. Of patients
who present to the hospital with an upper extremity amputation, 66% to 86% are not
candidates for revascularization or replantation and undergo revision amputation.5

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Traumatic amputations to the upper or lower extremities often result from high-energy
injuries.
Injury Classification
Classification of Open Fractures
The Gustilo-Anderson classification (Table 1) requires that surgical débridement be performed
before assigning a type. All factors are considered in assigning the type; however, the highest
possible type typically should be assigned based on each factor.

Injury Scoring Systems
Modern injury scoring systems are not predictive of amputation and should not be used in
isolation to determine the need for amputation in the limb at risk.8
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History

Patient History
Surgeons must determine the mechanism of injury, the level of wound contamination,
whether a crush injury was present, and ischemia time because these factors affect not
only surgical timing but also overall patient outcomes. Surgeons also must understand
the energy (high energy versus low energy) imparted to the patient and their soft tissues
because soft-tissue injury will evolve over 48 hours and even for a few days longer after
a crush injury. Therefore, tissue that seemed viable initially may be necrotic on
subsequent débridement.

Comorbid conditions, including tobacco smoking status, malnutrition, and peripheral
vascular disease, also adversely affect outcomes.9-11
Finally, recent data have demonstrated the effects of several factors on outcomes,
including patient education level, access to care, and social-support network, among
others. Identifying these factors early in the patient’s recovery process may allow for
targeted intervention to optimize outcomes, if appropriate.11,12
Physical Examination

Physical Examination
The patient’s overall physiologic status must be assessed because it is important to
consider in the acute decision-making process for the limb at risk. Hemorrhage must be
controlled with the use of a compression dressing or tourniquet if necessary. The soft
tissues should be inspected for wound size, location, and overall zone of injury. Skin
integrity should be assessed for the presence of burns, abrasions, lacerations, and
ecchymosis. Finally, the muscle also should be examined for viability.
Neurovascular Examination

Neurovascular Examination
A thorough neurovascular examination should be performed in the limb at risk,
including the ankle-brachial index (ABI) if appropriate. An ABI less than 0.9 indicates a
potential vascular injury and warrants additional evaluation. If the patient has a vascular
injury, revascularization should be performed within 6 hours because warm ischemia of
more than 6 hours results in irreversible changes, including necrosis of muscle and
nerve. Note that the absence of plantar sensation on presentation in the limb at risk
should not be used as an indication for amputation. Many nerve injuries will continue to
recover for years after injury. Bosse et al13 followed 55 patients with absent plantar

sensation on presentation after high-energy lower extremity trauma, comparing those
who underwent amputation (n = 25) and those who underwent limb salvage (n = 29) with
a matched control group with normal sensation (n = 29). The authors found that the
insensate salvage and sensate control group had a similar percentage of patients with
normal plantar sensation at a follow-up of 2 years (55%). Only one patient in the
insensate salvage group had absent plantar sensation at final follow-up.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
In any patient in whom a fracture is suspected, AP and lateral radiographs of the affected area
and radiographs that include the joints above and below the affected area should be obtained.
These radiographs should be obtained as soon as possible to facilitate preoperative planning.
In the upper extremity, radiographs of the limb with the amputated part may aid in the
decision to perform replantation or amputation. The amount of bone remaining in the limb
also will guide future reconstruction efforts. If preserved, the thumb metacarpal may be
lengthened to provide a longer post for pinch. If an amputation involves the elbow,
preservation of the distal humeral condyles may facilitate prosthetic fitting. If amputation is
more proximal, a flexion osteotomy of the distal humerus may be performed to improve
prosthetic fit.14,15 In addition, a minimum of 5 cm of bone distal to a joint is required for
prosthetic suspension and preservation of joint function.16
Computed Tomography
CT is ordered as clinically indicated to assess articular fractures and to determine ability for
reconstruction.
Other Studies
Angiography is performed based on clinical suspicion of vascular injury, the type of injury, and
the following indications:
Knee dislocation (or equivalent; eg, medial tibial plateau fracture) with asymmetric pulses
and ABI less than 0.9
A cool, pale foot with poor distal capillary refill

Decision-Making Process: Limb Salvage Versus Amputation

Decision-Making Process: Limb Salvage Versus Amputation
Several common misperceptions exist regarding the debate on limb salvage versus
amputation. The first is that a patient with a limb at risk should undergo amputation if
he or she has absent plantar sensation. Bosse et al13 reported a similar percentage
(55%) of patients had normal plantar sensation 2 years after a limb-threatening injury
regardless of group: insensate patients who underwent limb salvage compared with
sensate patients who underwent limb salvage.
Another common misconception is that scoring systems can replace clinical decision
making to accurately predict limbs that should be amputated and limbs that should be
salvaged. Several studies have demonstrated the futility of scoring systems used to
predict successful limb salvage. In a prospective observational study of more than 500
patients who sustained high-energy lower extremity trauma, Ly et al8 found that current
scoring systems, including the Mangled Extremity Severity Score; the Limb Salvage Index;
the Predictive Salvage Index; the Nerve Injury, Ischemia, Soft Tissue Injury, Skeletal
Injury, Shock, and Age of Patient Score; and the Hannover Fracture Scale-97, were not
predictive of amputation.
In considering costs, limb salvage typically results in higher initial costs than amputation;
however, MacKenzie et al17 found that, although 2-year costs were similar (salvage,
$81,316; amputation, $91,106), the projected lifetime costs, including purchase and
maintenance of the prosthesis, was more than three times higher after trauma-related
amputation (salvage, $163,282; amputation, $509,275). This is partly because of the
relatively young age of traumatic amputees, who have higher physical demands and the
need for lifetime prosthetic care.

Finally, those undergoing amputation often have been thought to have better outcomes
than those undergoing limb salvage. In a prospective observational study of more than
500 patients who sustained high-energy lower extremity trauma, no difference in
outcomes using the Sickness Impact Profile were noted 2- and 7-year follow-up between
those who underwent limb salvage and those who underwent amputation. Several
factors were predictive of poor outcome regardless of group: rehospitalization for a
major complication, low education level, nonwhite race, poverty, lack of private health
insurance, poor social-support network, low self-efficacy, and involvement in disability-
compensation litigation.12,18
After an upper extremity amputation, the decision to perform replantation or revision
amputation may depend on several injury and patient factors. First, the level of injury is
important. Patients with a major upper extremity amputation (nondigit) who undergo
successful replantation ultimately have better long-term patient-reported outcomes
than those who undergo amputation at the same level.19 Generally accepted indications
for replantation include a thumb amputation, amputation through the level of the palm
or proximal, pediatric amputation at any level, and multiple-digit amputation. Isolated
digit amputations distal to the flexor digitorum superficialis insertion lead to better
results if replanted compared with amputations at more proximal levels and currently
are accepted as a relative indication for replantation.20 The mechanism of injury can
determine if replantation is feasible. Parts that are severely crushed or mangled indicate
amputation.21 Ischemia time is an important consideration in patient with an upper
extremity amputation. For major limb amputations, warm ischemia time of 2 to 4 hours
or cold ischemia time of 6 to 8 hours is required because of a larger proportion of
muscle that is ischemia-sensitive. In the digit, successful replantation has been reported
with warm ischemia time of 10 to 12 hours or cold ischemia of as long as 24 hours.
Patient factors, such as age, comorbidities, and work status, should be considered.
Replantation surgery may involve prolonged anesthesia, blood transfusion, and acidosis
that may not be tolerated by patients who have other injuries or considerable
comorbidities. Patients who undergo major limb replantation in the upper extremity
frequently do not return to work until 2 years postoperatively, and patients who undergo
replantation of a digit may require 4 to 12 months before returning to work.22,23 This
may not be acceptable to some patients because return to work may be sooner after an

amputation; as soon as 1 to 2 months in patients who undergo digital completion
amputation.22 Social factors and support also are important considerations because
substantial rehabilitation is required for a positive outcome, and patient motivation may
be critical to obtaining satisfactory results.
In a retrospective cohort study of 324 military service members who sustained a limb-
threatening injury and underwent amputation or limb salvage, Doukas et al24 found that
those who underwent a lower extremity amputation tended to have better outcomes
than those who underwent limb salvage; however, an element of selection bias existed
that may have favored the amputee patient population. A follow-up study evaluating
differences in military service members with similar upper extremity injuries found no
difference between upper extremity amputation or limb salvage.25
Surgical Management
General principles in performing trauma-related amputation include the following:
Aggressive initial surgical débridement, with plan to return to the operating room for repeat
débridement and definitive closure when the soft tissues are ready
If the amputation is performed through the zone of injury acutely, the wound typically is left
open and managed with the use of moist gauze or negative-pressure dressings, with
definitive closure delayed to ensure the tissues within the zone of injury remain healthy and
viable. Use caution in applying a negative-pressure dressing acutely to a massive fresh
wound bed because this may result in excessive bleeding.
Preserve length and soft tissues if viable during initial débridement to allow for more
reconstruction options at the time of definitive closure/amputation.
Save functional joint levels if possible. This includes consideration for stabilizing a proximal
fracture to provide an optimal, more functional residual limb.26
Identify and manage all named nerves via gentle dissection, sharp proximal transection, and
retraction into an area without surrounding pressure.
Identify, isolate, and ligate all named vessels, avoiding group ligation.
Bevel and smooth all bone ends if appropriate.
Perform a stable myodesis under physiologic tension if appropriate for the level of
amputation.

Ensure adequate distal soft-tissue padding. Ideally, robust soft tissue composed of muscle
with full-thickness skin is present.
Indications
The level of amputation often is performed to salvage the most distal joint possible for optimal
function.
Common Levels for Upper and Lower Extremity Amputations
Transmetatarsal Amputation

Transmetatarsal Amputation
Other less common partial foot amputations and disarticulations are shown in Figure 1
and 2. This amputation level is associated with excellent long-term function and
decreased energy expenditure during ambulation compared with amputation at more
proximal levels. Careful attention to the soft tissues preoperatively is important because
a viable long posterior, plantar flap is ideal for soft-tissue closure and successful wound
healing.
The dorsal incision extends from the midshaft level of the first metatarsal to the
midshaft of the fifth metatarsal. The transverse dorsal incision then extends
longitudinally toward the respective metatarsal heads. The plantar transverse incision is
made along the metatarsal heads to connect the limbs of the incision.
The dorsalis pedis and the branches of the posterior tibial artery are identified and
ligated. The superficial peroneal nerve, deep peroneal nerve, and branches of the tibial
nerve are transected sharply. The flexor and extensor tendons are cut with care to
ensure the insertion of the anterior tibial tendon, peroneal longus, and peroneal brevis
remain intact to balance the foot.
The metatarsals are resected with the use of an oscillating saw after a gentle cascade at
the level of the skin incision. The bone ends are smoothed, and the plantar flap is

Achilles tendon lengthening should be considered to minimize the risk of an equinus
contracture after partial foot amputation. In addition, if a more proximal foot
amputation is performed, such as a Lisfranc or Chopart level, transfer of the tibialis
anterior should be performed to prevent an equinovarus deformity, and Achilles tendon
lengthening is essential.

hindfoot, ankle, and distal tibia that is not reconstructible. All efforts should be made to
salvage the knee joint if possible (Videos 1 and 2; Figures 3 and 4).

The ideal length of the residual limb is 2.5 cm for every 30 cm of height, which typically
equates to between 12.5 and 17.5 cm distal to the knee joint line.27 In addition, although
a minimum of 8 cm of length must be proximal to the heel pad, an amputation level of
27 to 28 cm above the heel pad will allow for adequate fitting of modern prostheses.28,29
The transverse skin incision typically is made 1 to 2 cm distal to the proposed tibial bone
cut if a standard posterior flap is used. This incision extends from 1 cm posterior to the
medial border of the tibia to the fibula laterally. The incision then extends distally along
the posteromedial border of the tibia and the posterior border of the fibula. Various
lengths for the posterior flap have been recommended, including the length of the
diameter of the limb plus 1 to 2 cm (standard posterior flap) or 5 cm (extended posterior
flap) or a length approximately twice the transverse incision length or twice the
circumference of the calf.30-32 The goal is to have a reasonable length of the posterior
flap because it often has a more robust blood supply to improve healing of the surgical
incision. A large posterior flap also places the suture line anteriorly and proximal to the
end-bearing surface, which may improve stump durability and prosthetic fitting and
wear.
The anterior and lateral compartments are transected at the level of the skin incision
anteriorly. The anterior tibial artery is doubly ligated, and the superficial and deep
peroneal nerves are transected. Medially, the saphenous vein is ligated, and the nerve
transected. The sural nerve is identified, and a traction neurectomy performed.
The tibial bone cut is performed, beveling the anterior crest to minimize the bony
prominence to aid prosthetic fitting. The fibula is then cut no more than 1 cm proximal
to the tibia, beveling from proximal lateral to distal medial. The amputation knife can be
used to cut through the deep posterior compartment musculature, exiting at the
posterior incision. After the leg is removed, the tibial neurovascular bundle is identified,
the artery is again doubly ligated, and a traction neurectomy is performed, ensuring that
the tibial nerve has been dissected free from the vessels.

The bone bridge is a modification of the transtibial amputation in which the distal fibula
is secured to the distal tibia. Multiple surgical techniques have been described; however,
the functional benefit remains a subject of controversy.33-35 Regardless, overt clinical or
radiographic evidence of fibular instability is a commonly accepted indication for this


Knee Disarticulation

for end-bearing, a longer lever arm, and an intact adductor magnus; however, it also is

A transverse incision is made midway between the inferior pole of the patella and the
tibial tubercle and is carried medial and lateral to the midpoint of the knee, at which the

The skin incision is taken down to fascia circumferentially, and the saphenous vein is
ligated as a traction neurectomy is performed on the saphenous nerve. Medial and
lateral incisions are made along the patellar tendon, which is transected at the level of its
insertion onto the tibial tubercle. The knee retinaculum is then cut to its midpoint
medially and laterally, and the anterior cruciate ligament is detached from its insertion
on the tibia. As the tibia is subluxed anteriorly, the posterior cruciate ligament is
released from its tibial insertion, and the remaining capsule is cut.
Blunt dissection between the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles allows for identification
and clamping of the popliteal artery and veins. The amputation is completed, and the
artery is doubly ligated with the use of a stick-tie and simple ligature. The tibial and
common peroneal nerves are identified, and traction neurectomies are performed. The
medial sural nerve also is identified in the posterior flap, and a traction neurectomy
performed.
Removal of the patella is based on surgeon discretion. The authors of this lesson prefer
to retain the patella for improved prosthetic fitting. The patellar tendon is then anchored
to the cruciate ligaments with the use of a heavy, nonabsorbable suture. The medial and
lateral hamstring tendons can then be sutured to the adjacent joint capsule.
The remaining gastrocnemius muscle is then used to cover the distal end of the femur.
Often, the medial head of the gastrocnemius muscle is all that is necessary and can
provide adequate coverage if it is rotated over the end of the distal femur and secured
to the joint capsule and the patellar tendon anteriorly. The posterior flap is then sutured
closed with or without drains based on surgeon discretion.

Transfemoral Amputation

Transfemoral Amputation

Hand and Digit Amputation

Hand and Digit Amputation
Fingertip amputations are relatively common, and treatment can be tailored to patient
and injury characteristics. For amputations with pulp loss and no exposed bone, primary
closure or healing via secondary intention may be performed. In fact, most amputated
fingertip wounds can heal within 4 to 6 weeks. After a fingertip amputation that is
managed via secondary intention, two-point discrimination generally recovers to 3 to 6
mm, and 85% of laborers return to normal duty within 1 month.37,38 Other options
include skin grafting, local flaps, or regional flaps. The Atasoy-Kleinert V-Y advancement
flap is ideal for dorsal oblique or transverse amputations and can be advanced as much
as 1 cm over a defect. For volar oblique amputations, the Kutler lateral V-Y flap may be
performed but with only approximately 3 to 4 mm of coverage.39 Regional flaps are
other effective options for volar tissue loss and include the cross-finger flap and the
thenar flap. These flaps require a second surgical procedure after 3 to 4 weeks for flap
division.
Preservation of digit length is a primary consideration in patients with a thumb
amputation, because the thumb is commonly thought to contribute to approximately
40% of overall hand function. The Moberg flap is a versatile local flap to preserve thumb
length if the defect is less than 2 cm. In this flap, a volar skin flap, including the
neurovascular bundles, is created through midaxial incisions and advanced. Even if soft-

the thick palmar skin can provide effective soft-tissue coverage. At this level, fitting a

associated with the benefit of functioning well in assistance to the other limb.42
Transradial amputations are the most common level of major upper extremity
amputation. Bony resection is performed approximately 8 to 10 cm proximal to the wrist
joint to allow for adequate muscle coverage and optimal prosthesis fitting. Proximally, 5
cm or more of bone is required distal to the elbow to provide adequate support for
prosthetic joint suspension.16 In more proximal forearm amputations, the biceps tendon
may be transferred to the ulna to decrease the risk of a flexion contracture.42 A fish-
mouth incision may be performed, and a myodesis of the deep volar compartment to
the radius and ulna can be performed, followed by myoplasty of the superficial flexor
and extensor muscles. The radial and ulnar arteries are identified, and suture is ligated
proximal to the level of the bony amputation.
Targeted muscle reinnervation (TMR) or regenerative peripheral nerve interfaces may be
considered at the forearm level. By selectively transferring the amputated median and
ulnar nerves to partially amputated or redundant muscles, more myoelectric signals can
be created to increase prosthetic function. In addition, TMR offers a prophylactic
measure against neuroma formation for mixed motor and sensory nerves in the
forearm. If TMR is performed, surgeons must thin the subcutaneous fat overlying muscle
groups for easier myoelectric signal transmission.

Postoperative Management

Postoperative Management
For lower extremity amputations, soft dressings usually are applied with splinting, if
necessary, to avoid potential contractures. For example, after a transmetatarsal
amputation, a splint can be placed with the ankle in neutral to minimize the risk of
equinus contracture. After the first dressing change, if the incision is dry and healing
well, elastic dressings or shrinkers commonly are used to help control edema, shaping
the limb for subsequent prosthetic fitting. Knee flexion contractures can develop in
transtibial amputees, and hip flexion contractures can develop in transfemoral
amputees. Transtibial amputees must maintain knee extension with early range of
motion or splinting in extension if necessary and must spend time in the prone position
(tummy time) to maintain hip extension.
For upper extremity amputations, an elastic dressing is placed after the wound is healed,
followed by a simple terminal end device that serves to decrease residual limb edema
and improve prosthetic use. After the limb edema stabilizes, definitive prosthesis fitting

Complications
A complication associated with the amputation develops in as many as 51% of patients
with trauma-related amputation. In addition, the Lower Extremity Assessment Project
Study Group reported that as many as 30% of patients are re-hospitalized and 14.5% of
patients require revision of the residual limb after trauma-related amputation.1 The
most common indications for revision surgery after traumatic amputation include
infection, symptomatic heterotopic ossification, and neuroma.44

At 2 years postamputation, as many as 7% of patients do not have fully healed wounds.
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy

Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Any time a nerve is injured, whether from trauma or the amputation itself, a risk for
neuroma exists. In patients with isolated peripheral nerve injuries without amputation,
the incidence of neuroma formation is 5% to 10%; however, this increases to 50% if an
amputation occurs.45,46 A neuroma is defined as a disorganized growth of axons,
Schwann cells, macrophages, and other neurocellular material that leads to abnormal
regeneration and irregular branching of axons. Over time, spontaneous axonal activity
occurs with altered pain perception and, eventually, central nervous system
changes.47,48

Until recently, no accepted criteria for the diagnosis of a neuroma were accepted, which
made developing effective treatment options difficult. After an amputation, a
symptomatic neuroma may be diagnosed if pain is neuropathic in nature (burning,
sharp, shooting, electric, paresthesia, numbness, cold intolerance) and in a defined
neural anatomic distribution. In addition, the patient must have a positive Tinel sign, a
positive response to a local anesthetic injection, or advanced imaging studies that
confirm a neuroma.45
After a neuroma has formed, medical management often is the first line of treatment;
this includes medications, therapy, and injections. Traditionally, surgical management of
named nerves, either prophylactically or after neuroma formation, has consisted of a
traction neurectomy. Traction neurectomy effectively changes the environment in which
a free nerve ending may exist so that it is less prone to be symptomatic; however, a
neuroma may still form. Prior studies have shown that the occurrence or recurrence of
neuroma after traction neurectomy may be relatively high, as high as 23% to 42% in the
upper and lower extremities.49,50 Other similar approaches that alter the nerve-ending
environment, termed passive treatment options, include excision and implantation into
muscle, bone, or vein; relocation nerve grafting; nerve capping; and centro-central
assisted neurorrhaphy.
Recently, interest in active treatment options that inhibit neuroma formation by
providing a free nerve ending a target has increased. In the setting of an amputation,
this typically involves TMR or regenerative peripheral nerve interfaces. TMR works by
directing the free nerve ending to a denervated muscle, providing an end target. In the
setting of an amputation, muscles that have lost their distal insertion site but have a
preserved vascular supply can be reinnervated with the amputated nerve. Instead of
following the pathway to forming a neuroma, the free nerve ending then targets the
denervated muscle. Regenerative peripheral nerve interfaces work in a manner similar
to that of TMR, in that they provide a distal target for an injured, regenerating free nerve
end. In this technique, a nerve end is implanted into a small piece of free muscle graft
obtained from an amputated limb or nearby tissue. Outcomes of both techniques show
are associated with 70% to 100% reduction of postamputation neuroma pain and
substantial reduction in phantom limb pain.51-55

Rehabilitation
Traumatic amputees often require multidisciplinary resources, including physical medicine,
rehabilitation, prosthetics, physical therapy, and mental health, for optimal recovery.
Metabolic Cost of Walking after Amputation

Metabolic Cost of Walking after Amputation
The more proximal the level of amputation, the more energy is expended during
walking. For example, the energy expended for a unilateral transfemoral amputee may
be as much as 60% greater than that of an able-bodied individual, whereas the energy
expended for a transtibial amputee during ambulation may be as much as 30% greater
than that of an able-bodied individual.56,57 Recent data suggest that, in younger patients
who have access to modern prosthetics and advanced rehabilitation, the energy
requirement for ambulation is much better; for transtibial amputees, the energy
requirement for ambulation is comparable to that expended during ambulation in able-
bodied individuals.58,59
